summary: Moritz Johner describes PatchPilot, Form3's automated CVE remediation system addressing a never-ending backlog across thousands of repositories. Traditional tools like Dependabot and Renovate only handle manifest-level bumps, missing CVEs in base image OS packages, downloaded binaries, and cascading changes like Go runtime bumps requiring linter updates. PatchPilot uses a two-layer architecture: a deterministic Go controller that discovers vulnerable OCI images, scans them, maps them to repositories, and controls all dangerous operations including GitHub write access and CI triggers; and an agent layer that performs minimal effective patches, remediates CI failures, and verifies its own work—but only edits files on disk, never committing or pushing. The flow starts with an assessment manifest, clones the repo, invokes the CVE remediation agent, vets changes deterministically for stray artifacts, commits and creates a PR, watches CI, and loops on PR remediation until success or retry-limit-triggered human escalation. Agent retrospectives after each invocation are aggregated to identify infrastructure issues and repository complexity problems at scale. The central thesis emerged from Infosec scrutiny: a useful coding agent with production credentials is inherently a supply chain actor requiring engineer-equivalent guardrails. A single PR bumping dependencies changed 70,000 lines, creating an enormous prompt injection attack surface. Mitigations include prompt steering—telling the agent which directories like vendor dirs and CI logs contain untrusted data—and end-to-end eval repositories with crafted injection vectors like deprecated functions that try to recruit the agent. The Docker socket was the critical unsolved problem: giving it to the agent so it can build and verify Dockerfiles means a prompt injection could spawn a privileged container, read process memory, plant SSH keys—game over. Linux sandboxing tools (landlock, bubble wrap, seccomp, Kaniko, buildkit) don't compose well with Docker sockets. The solution: run everything inside a Firecracker microVM with its own kernel, where the Docker daemon and agent are contained. Separate network policies apply to each layer via a DNS/TCP forwarder inside the microVM, with all traffic flowing through a Vsock to a host process that enforces hostname, port, and CIDR rules. A custom CA can enable TLS interception. Johner notes existing agent sandboxes (Codex, Claude) are worthless with Docker socket access, and recommends the open-source Micro Sandbox project (YC-funded) as the best current option if rebuilding today. He observes most sandbox-as-a-service vendors lack Docker socket containment and proper network controls, and the ecosystem is still beta-phase with a gap before enterprise readiness. The final architectural principle: the blast radius of an agent is an architecture decision—what's deterministic versus agentic IS the security model.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: The Dependency Patching Problem
sections.summary: Johner introduces dependency patching as an unglamorous, never-ending backlog at Form3's scale of thousands of repositories. Traditional tools like Dependabot and Renovate only handle manifest-level bumps, missing CVEs in base image OS packages and downloaded binaries, and cannot reason about cascading changes such as Go runtime bumps requiring linter updates that introduce new linting rules.

sections.title: PatchPilot Architecture and the Supply Chain Thesis
sections.summary: PatchPilot splits into a deterministic Go layer that discovers vulnerable artifacts, scans images, and maps them to repositories, and an agent layer for reasoning about CI failures and remediation. Infosec challenged whether this is automation or a supply chain incident. The thesis: a useful coding agent with production credentials becomes a supply chain actor requiring guardrails similar to those for human engineers.

sections.title: End-to-End PatchPilot Flow
sections.summary: The flow starts with an assessment manifest, clones the repo, invokes the CVE remediation agent for minimal effective changes, vets changes deterministically for stray artifacts, commits and creates a PR, watches CI, and if failures occur invokes a PR remediation agent in a loop until success or a retry limit triggers human escalation. The agent only modifies files on disk—never commits, pushes, or watches CI directly.

sections.title: Agent Retrospectives and Observability
sections.summary: After each agent invocation, the agent performs a short retrospective on what went well, what went wrong, missing tools, and needed context. Aggregating these across PRs reveals two issue categories: infrastructure-related (network failures, permission issues) and repository-complexity-related (hard-to-reason-about repos needing system prompt changes or repo-specific instructions). Observability for agents remains an open community problem.

sections.title: Production Example and Credential Split
sections.summary: Johner shows a production screenshot where the agent bumped a base image and updated libcrypto3 and libssl3, also removing previously pinned packages—a fix he might have missed manually. He details the capabilities given to PatchPilot: GitHub read/write, OCI registry credentials, runtimes, linters, network access. The critical split is that dangerous capabilities (GitHub write, CI triggers) are kept in the deterministic layer, never given to the agent.

sections.title: Prompt Injection Mitigation and the 70,000-Line Problem
sections.summary: The deterministic-agent boundary limits blast radius when the agent gets prompt injected. A single dependency bump PR changed 70,000 lines of code, creating a wide attack surface. Mitigations include prompt steering—telling the agent which directories like vendor dirs and CI logs contain untrusted data—and end-to-end eval repositories with crafted injection vectors such as deprecated functions that try to recruit the agent maliciously. Unknown injection vectors remain, so the system is not built on hope but on layered defense.

sections.title: The Docker Socket Problem and MicroVM Solution
sections.summary: The agent needs the Docker socket to build and verify Dockerfiles, but with it a prompt-injected agent can spawn privileged containers, read process memory, plant SSH keys—game over. They ran this way in production but it didn't feel good. Linux sandboxing tools (landlock, bubble wrap, seccomp, Kaniko, buildkit) don't compose well with Docker sockets. The solution: a Firecracker microVM with its own kernel containing the agent, Docker socket, and daemon, providing proper isolation.

sections.title: Per-Layer Network Policies and Sandbox Ecosystem
sections.summary: Separate network policies apply to the deterministic and agent layers via a DNS/TCP forwarder inside the microVM, with all traffic flowing through a Vsock to a host process enforcing hostname, port, and CIDR rules. A custom CA enables TLS interception. Existing agent sandboxes (Codex, Claude) are insufficient with Docker socket access. Johner recommends the open-source Micro Sandbox project (YC-funded) as the best current option, though most tooling remains beta-phase with gaps before enterprise readiness.

sections.title: Blast Radius as Architecture Decision
sections.summary: The final takeaway: blast radius of an agent is an architecture decision. Not giving the agent credentials for CI triggers, GitHub push, or PR creation—pushing that into the deterministic layer—caps the blast radius. What's deterministic versus agentic IS the security model. Johner invites the community to discuss production agent sandboxing, noting a dedicated sandbox panel the next day.
